First, we design an off-policy model-based RL algorithm, utilizing a neural network to approximate the reward function. Following this, we employ a bandit approach to select optimal configuration values. Our approach is tested on real-world data from an REN pilot in Japan and demonstrates the feasibility of improving REN positions via RL methods.

A multi-measurement approach combining LHCb results has been undertaken to determine the CKM angle gamma, utilizing various B-meson decays to Higgs bosons, charmed mesons, and unobserved b-quarks. The analysis incorporates three distinct measurements, including a determination of gamma's value as being 72$^{\circ}$ radiants with a 95% confidence level from a B0 decay to charmed mesons and photons, a 68^circ radiants with a 1 sigma uncertainty from a B+ decay to charmed mesons and unobserved b-quarks, and a determination of gamma's value as being 74.1 degrees with a 3.2 degree uncertainty from a B0 decay to Higgs bosons and unobserved b-quarks. The combined result of the three determinations yields a gamma value of 72.4 degree with a 2.4 degree uncertainty, aligning with Standard Model predictions.

Several properties of complex ellipsoids among convex bodies in n-dimensional space have been rigorously established in relation to their sections and projections, a crucial concept for further research. Establishing criteria for complex symmetry within this framework provides a valuable approach.

The collection, processing, and dissemination of personal data by large tech companies has raised significant consumer protection concerns, prompting the European Union to implement the General Data Protection Regulation. In contrast to traditional data markets, off-the-shelf solutions dominate the industry, leaving their users with limited control over their data. In our study, we created a platform allowing users to sell data to developers to overtake these intermediaries. A user study revealed that people value the privacy and financial benefits of data selling, but prefer the protection of traditional data markets. They also express anxiety about users sharing data or developing applications that exploit their personal information. Our study has implications for the development of data markets, specifically in regards to user-friendly interfaces, data management, and protection regulations.

A new approach to detect FTN signaling symbols uses deep learning-based List Sphere Decoding (DL-LSD). This method is applied to binary FSK with variable block-lengths and non-uniform sampling rates. Comparative analysis with existing methods, such as maximum-a-posteriori decoding and deep learning-based maximum likelihood decoding, reveals that DL-LSD outperforms in terms of bit error rate. Furthermore, a proposed convolutional neural network architecture significantly reduces the complexity of the DL-LSD algorithm by enabling the sharing of weights, leading to substantial reductions in total parameter count compared to the baseline models.

This paper explores two topological sequels, Order topology and Frink Ideal topology, in GAGA effect algebras with an abundance of atoms, demonstrating that these topologies are distinct and that Order topology is completely separated. We also prove that when both the Order topology and Frink Ideal topology are separable in a GAGA effect algebra, both topologies become discrete.

Recent advancements in deep learning models have achieved exceptional performance
in image classification tasks. Nevertheless, these models can be overconfident in
their predictions and exhibit poor generalization performance on unseen data.
To address this, we introduce SaliencyMix, a data augmentation technique based on
the saliency maps of an ensemble of pre-trained models. By generating masks for
data augmentation using these maps, we improve the model's ability to discern
reversible and irreversible transformations and thereby enhance its robustness.
Experimental results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K demonstrate that
SaliencyMix yields better generalization performance than traditional data
augmentation methods, achieving up to 2.5% improvement in top-1 accuracy.

The infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebras $\mathcal{H}_\infty(q)$ are defined as the inductive limit of their finite-dimensional counterparts, derived from the algebra of infinitely tiled diagonal matrices. These algebras have connections to symmetric groups, hyperoctahedral groups, and Weyl groups, among others. They can be extended to infinite-dimensional complex functions and have various properties, including being semisimple and artinian. In a specific paper, we explored the algebra's subalgebras and specific properties, such as the existence of unique maximal left and right ideals, as well as the traces associated with these modules.

A new method is proposed to investigate alternative gravity theories using galaxy shape information from weak lensing and intrinsic galaxy alignments. This is achieved by testing how galaxy shapes are correlated with their surrounding mass distributions. By combining intrinsic galaxy alignments with cosmic shear data, modified gravity theories can be tested without the biases that typically affect traditional galaxy shape measurements. A study of mock galaxy populations indicates that this method can be effective in distinguishing between modified and standard gravity, including the commonly modified Horndeski's reduced gravity theory. This method can be implemented in the LSST survey to constrain modified gravity using the ELVE pipeline.

We investigate the flow behavior of flexible, non-rigid particles that can change shape in response to forces, which leads to a diverse range of mechanical properties. Through numerical simulations, we observe that the particles can exhibit a range of behaviors, from a sudden transition from a fluid-like to a solid-like state as their volume is increased, and by analyzing how stress responds to strain, we find that the particles can exhibit a negative change in response to a positive change in strain, a phenomenon known as normal stress. We compare the normal stress to a measure of the particles' flexibility and find a simple relationship between the two, which allows us to explain the particles' behavior in terms of a single parameter that describes their structure, which can be verified experimentally.

The melting behavior of gold nanoparticles has been studied through molecular dynamics simulations and experimental verification. Despite significant attention from the scientific community, a comprehensive and experimentally-verified understanding of nanoparticle melting has yet to be established. Using a comprehensive, data-driven approach, we investigated the melting behavior of gold nanoparticles with a range of sizes (from 1.5 to 4.5 nm) and shapes (spherical, prismatic, and prolate spherical). Our simulations and experiments demonstrate that the melting temperature increases as the size decreases, with the melting temperature of small nanoparticles exceeding that of bulk material. We observed a transition from geometric to geometric-thermal melting modes as the size decreases, with the geometric melting mode becoming dominant in larger nanoparticles and geometric-thermal melting mode in smaller ones. The experimental results were found to be in good agreement with the simulated results, with the melting temperatures matching within 10%. The simulation results were found to be insensitive to the force field used, providing a reliable prediction of melting behavior. The experimental results were found to be highly consistent across different force fields. The comprehensive dataset collected in this study can be utilized for future studies and applications.

This is the beginning of a series focused on the generalizations and uses of well-known theorems within variational bifurcation theory. Leveraging parameterized versions of splitting theorems in Morse theory, some prominent bifurcation theorems are broadened for potential operators by relaxing conventional requirements for the differentiability of associated functionals and operators. This generalized framework is crucial in examining bifurcations of solutions for non-differentiable (such as discontinuous) operators, where standard theories are insufficient. The key application of these theorems lies in the analysis of bifurcations of solutions for non-differentiable operators, often encountered in significant physical phenomena like nonlinear wave propagation and vibrations. The results have far-reaching implications in examining bifurcations of solutions for nonlinear electro-magnetics and nonlinear elasticity.

The model known as Tetrahedron of flavors successfully predicts the masses of all 12 ordinary quark masses, including the mass of the b-quark, up to an insignificant level of precision, without any prior knowledge of their values. It achieves this by utilizing a simple and mathematically based approach, drawing from the fundamental principles of quantum field theories that are minimally extended. This model serves as a potential alternative to the Standard Model of particle physics, featuring a simplified Yukawa sector with a unique, parameter-free structure that incorporates negative and positive quark masses in a specific ratio.
We derive alternative representations of (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials using the fermionic p-adic q-integral on Zp, in conjunction with weighted q-Bernstein polynomials.

In various fields such as healthcare, education, and social welfare, dynamic decision-making plays a significant role. Researchers often examine the impact of interventions on policy makers' decision-making behaviors, particularly how their long-term actions affect future well-being or outcomes. Due to the difficulty in measuring unobservable factors like preferences and population characteristics, researchers must rely on such measures to accurately assess the effects of interventions. This paper presents a new framework that utilizes reinforcement learning to analyze sequential decision-making processes and proposes a novel method for estimating long-term effects in dynamic settings. Our approach accounts for missing data at decision points, allowing for a comprehensive analysis. This framework offers a general framework for analyzing complex decision-making processes and can be adapted to various real-world applications. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this framework using a simulation study and a real-world example from a large-scale social assistance program in South Africa.

To assess the link between past exposure and a disease in a population, researchers conduct case-control studies. However, participants' recollections of past events are often biased, which can distort the estimates of exposure prevalence among cases versus controls. This paper explores how to account for such biases to identify the exposure-disease relationship. It presents a method involving a counterfactual framework and a participant-level adjustment that removes bias from the analysis. This approach is applied to the Avon Longitudinal Study of Children, a large, well-documented cohort that tracks individuals from birth to age 34. Healthy young adults were asked about their early life exposure to pets and its effect on later asthma. We calculated the exposure prevalence among case and control groups and assessed bias using the exposure prevalence among a subpopulation with known life situation. We then proposed a method to adjust for bias at the individual level and to estimate the exposure prevalence among cases and controls. We compared this approach to a method using the exposure prevalence among entire cohorts of cases and controls. We found that bias was significant, and our proposed method produced a more accurate estimate of exposure prevalence among cases and controls. This, in turn, led to a smaller estimated risk of asthma due to exposure. We also found that ignoring bias caused overestimated the exposure prevalence among cases and overestimated the exposure prevalence among controls. This led to a biased estimate of the exposure-risk association.

Generative autoencoders, a type of probabilistic model, are often trained using maximum likelihood, yet their exact training methods are hindered due to the lack of inverse mappings for many used layers. This limitation, however, can be overcome by utilizing specific invertible and differentiable building blocks, thus enabling the exact maximum likelihood training of generative autoencoders. This research presents an exact maximum likelihood training framework for generative autoencoders, incorporating invertible layers, along with its theoretical underpinnings. Furthermore, it introduces a new, highly efficient and scalable invertible layer design, referred to as batch norm invertible kernel layers, which outperforms state-of-the-art layers in terms of computational efficiency and scalability. This new layer is then utilized to construct a generative autoencoder, demonstrating its capability to train and generate efficiently, even with large datasets.

Smart city monitoring involves tracking various urban indicators, such as environmental conditions and population demographics, over time. Deciding which data to collect and how to use it effectively is crucial for administrators. However, city data often exhibits correlations due to underlying patterns. For instance, higher temperatures may lead to increased water usage and higher air pollution levels. This requires smart city administrators to analyze and visualize data in a way that highlights these correlations. Existing approaches fall short in this area, failing to provide a practical solution for administrators. This paper proposes an innovative framework for visualizing correlated data in visual exploration tools. Our approach is designed to enhance smart city administrators' understanding of these correlations by highlighting key interconnected factors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through case studies and a prototype, and our methodology can be applied to other areas where correlated data is a significant factor.

This paper explores various forms of optimal geometric multigrid preconditioners for static condensation-based finite element schemes for the reaction-diffusion equation and the generalized Stokes equations. We consider the P0 finite element space for the Lagrange multiplier and polynomial finite element spaces of degree $r+1$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ or $r+2$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with $r$ being the polynomial degree for the unknown flux. Our study reveals that the resulting preconditioned iterative solvers exhibit an optimal convergence rate of $O(r^{3/2})$, independent of the physical parameters. This paper presents a detailed analysis of the preconditioner's norm and the proof of its optimal convergence for the reaction-diffusion equation and the generalized Stokes equations. We also provide an extensive numerical experiment section to verify the theoretical analysis.

A new Bayesian approach to sensitivity analysis is developed for handling missing data, focusing on estimating causal relationships influenced by data absence. In contrast to traditional frequentist methods, Bayesian sensitivity analysis enables the integration of prior knowledge to inform the analysis and quantify uncertainty through probability distributions. A corresponding method is proposed to calculate the E-value, a metric that assesses the evidence supporting a causal link under various data missingness scenarios. This innovative approach is adaptable to different Bayesian models and can be applied to multiple missing data types, outperforming existing methods in simulation studies.

In crossover trials with missing gene expression data, a multivariate repeated-measure mixed-effects model is used to analyze the data efficiently. This type of model accounts for the structure of the missing data, specifically in gene expression studies where multivariate responses are expected to exhibit positive dependence. An exact likelihood approach is developed to estimate model parameters, with a corresponding EM algorithm used for computational efficiency. However, a more straightforward method based on conditional likelihood is also proposed for simpler calculations. The effectiveness of the likelihood-based methods is demonstrated through a simulation study and are further illustrated with an actual gene expression data set.

This study develops a method for calculating the Stasheff A(n) combinatorial space 
by analyzing sequences with the Stasheff flag, drawing from a category equipped with 
a weak monoidal structure. This approach encompasses Stasheff A(n) and yields new 
underlying conditions for a weak monoidal structure. Additionally, it examines the 
relationship between Stasheff A(n) and the Stasheff flag sequences through group 
actions.

DRAM is the dominant memory technology in modern computing, but its performance often falls short due to inherent constraints. To address this, numerous studies have proposed in-DRAM optimizations for specific applications and functions. However, developing such optimizations is typically reserved for researchers with in-depth knowledge of DRAM hardware, making it challenging for application developers to create custom in-memory functions and optimizations. This paper introduces CODIC, an accessible platform that enables users to easily create custom in-DRAM functions, such as DRAM read and write operations, by providing a low-level abstraction of DRAM operations. CODIC provides a flexible framework that allows users to create custom in-DRAM functions through a software development kit. By integrating CODIC with popular DRAM simulators, users can simulate and test their in-DRAM functions before deployment. To demonstrate the flexibility and performance of CODIC, we developed two in-DRAM functions: DRAM row reconstruction and data pipelining for PCIe SSDs, which achieved significant improvements in read throughput of up to 1.3x and 1.2x respectively, with minimal storage overhead.

This research paper is the final installment of a series exploring the role of functional programming in managing and orchestrating virtualized networks. By harnessing the capabilities of a generic virtualized platform, researchers have developed a comprehensive framework for analyzing and optimizing network behavior. A novel approach to network design is proposed, grounded in functional programming and information theory, enabling the creation of highly adaptable network solutions. A prototype virtual network platform was developed to test the practicality of designing networks for diverse applications and environments using a unified design approach. The results were promising, indicating that this methodology can be scaled up to design complex networks, as demonstrated by the successful development of a virtual network platform capable of handling both wireless Ad Hoc and Time-Synchronized Cramer-Rainville non-disruptive networks.

This research assesses the effectiveness of single-qubit rotations on pairs and triplets of qubits in a two-dimensional surface encoded with the toric code, examining how these operations impact decoding thresholds from the perspective of information theory. We utilize a Monte Carlo simulation to analyze how these operations influence the toric code's decoding threshold when supplemented with partial measurements as they relate to classical information processing. We discovered that, although a standard single-qubit rotation does not enhance the toric code's decoding threshold, there is potential for improvement when using more complex multi-qubit gates. We found that, in a real-world setting where noise is not perfectly random, a specific type of entangling gate can boost the decoding threshold. We also investigated the influence of these gates on a more complex error correction code based on a planar surface of the hyperbolic plane coded with the hypercode, and observed similar effects.

The OPUS system is an extension of the VOPortal's job control module, designed for managing and controlling jobs at the Polish Astronomical Center's HPC facility.  Its architecture complies with Grid and Grid-Fortran protocols, utilising standards-based tools such as as job launcher based on Globus GRAM, connected via Grid-in-a-Box, and integrated with the VO's data management system via TWS WMS services.  A key feature is seamless integration with the VO's data management system via TWS WMS services, enabling the tracking of job status in relation to dataset availability.  Additionally, the OPUS system includes an educational module for novice users, encompassing tutorials and online courses on basic concepts in astronomy, use of astronomical databases, software tools, data analysis and more.

The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to an increase in the number of devices connected to the internet, resulting in more complex networks that require advanced management strategies. These sophisticated networks rely on various protocols to manage their operation, and understanding these protocols is essential to ensure efficient network performance. However, students often struggle to grasp protocol concepts, as they lack real-world applications and hands-on experience. Our research involves the development of a digital game that simulates a protocol stack, allowing students to interactively explore and understand protocol usage. Our initial results indicate that using our game in conjunction with traditional education significantly enhances students' comprehension of protocol-related concepts, as measured by significant increases in average scores.

The scenario of a H2-rich atmosphere, devoid of a protective atmosphere, is a common element of science fiction, but it is also a possibility in future human habitability scenarios. In such cases, the presence of ozone (O3) could potentially serve as a proxy for the atmospheric protection provided by oxygen (O2) that is essential for life. However, the O3 production efficiency can be influenced by various factors, including solar radiation, chemical reactivity, and photochemical conditions, which makes it challenging to assess the quality of the O3-O2 proxy in various environments. In a recent study, researchers simulated 100,000 photochemical models of an Earth-like atmosphere to determine how well the O3 and CO2 mixing ratios correlate with O2. The findings revealed that O3 is a reliable proxy for O2 in low-CO2, terrestrial atmosphere scenarios, but its accuracy diminishes in low-radiative forcing or high-CO2 environments. The study also showed that an optimal threshold for O3 is required to achieve high accuracy, but this threshold varies significantly depending on the conditions. The research suggests that O3 is a reliable proxy for O2 in an Earth-like atmosphere, but its effectiveness diminishes in low-radiative or high-CO2 environments.

The quantized Hall effect's extension to the Dirac model of matter reveals a novel state of matter characterized by the presence of one-dimensional currents confined to the system's surface, a phenomenon triggered by the magnetic field's periodic structure. This research demonstrates that the surface currents' behavior remains consistent even in the presence of various types of disorder. Additionally, it's shown that the surface currents' behavior in the presence of magnetic field modulations results in the emergence of a new phase with quantized, periodic variations of surface current intensity.

Multilingual neural machine translation (MNMT) plays a vital role in enabling language diversification and accelerating language development in information-rich fields. However, the integration of MNMT in specialized domains like law and medicine poses significant challenges, particularly in the case of limited target language data. This research examines the benefits of applying MNMT in the medical field, focusing on Spanish and English, where the scarcity of medical resources in the target language complicates the translation process. To address this issue, a comparative study was conducted to investigate the effects of fine-tuning MNMT models on medical texts. The results demonstrated that domain-specific adaptations enhance translation quality, particularly in the target language, and suggest that a hybrid approach, combining MNMT and domain fine-tuning, yields the most accurate translations.

A theoretical study of the propagation of various types of modified-acoustic waves in a four-component plasma, incorporating ion-temperature-range electrons, has been conducted. Different wave types such as solitons, shock waves, and pair shocks were identified and their conditions for existence were established. It was discovered that the presence of positive dust particles significantly modifies the properties of these waves, particularly in the case of positronically modified acoustic waves, where pair shocks and shock waves emerged with lower-than-critical ion temperature and higher ion-charge-density. However, this phenomenon was suppressed by the presence of positive dust particles. Furthermore, the study revealed that the wave speeds increase with dust charge density but decrease with increasing ion temperature. Interestingly, the study found that the wave speeds of shock waves are independent of electron charge-density but are influenced by the electron's temperature. The results also indicate that the wave speeds of positronically modified acoustic waves are dependent on both the ionic temperature and the charge-density of electrons. Additionally, the study found that the presence of dust particles has a significant impact on the wave speed in pair shocks and pair solitons, but has minimal effect on the wave speed in shock waves. Finally, the study found that the pair shocks and pair solitons, in the presence of dust particles, have higher speeds than their counterparts without dust particles, but the pair shocks and pair solitons, in the absence of dust particles, have higher speeds than their counterparts without dust particles, but the

The application of language models in neural information retrieval has been gaining traction, with a notable example being the Multilingual Dense Retrieval (MDR) approach that achieves impressive results in cross-lingual and cross-language retrieval tasks. However, its performance in these tasks often falls behind that of English-based models, despite being trained on data from 100 languages. To address this issue, we propose an unsupervised, context-aware approach, Context-based Adaptive Sentence for Language Modeling (CASL), which can be used to enhance the performance of multilingual dense retrieval models. By utilizing masked language modeling and focusing on both word-level and contextual information, CASL proves to be an effective means of improving dense retrieval systems. When combined with MDR, CASL significantly enhances the model's performance in cross-language and cross-lingual retrieval tasks, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art achievements.

Multimodal learning, which combines information from various sources like images and text, is hindered by imbalanced data, a problem that's been largely overlooked in the research. To address this, we introduce a groundbreaking approach that simultaneously identifies and rectifies these imbalances. Firstly, we identify the root cause of the problem by analyzing the relationships between different modalities, revealing that their dependencies are non-linear and non-additive. This means simply averaging values from one modality when it dominates the others can lead to inaccurate and irrelevant results. Next, we develop a novel loss function that effectively balances values from different modalities, a task that's complicated by the fact that these values are often represented differently. To overcome this hurdle, we use a prototypical-based approach, which allows us to compare and contrast different modalities more meaningfully. We've successfully tested our approach on multiple multimodal datasets, a novel benchmark for evaluating imbalanced learning, and the results show that it significantly outperforms competing methods, including those capable of learning from imbalanced data.

Using the Wigner function formalism, we've developed a transport model that accounts for the influence of vector interactions. The resulting equations exhibit an explicit solvable nature, as they align with the Vlasov equation when vector potentials are negligible. Derivations of the equilibrium and quasiparticle distribution functions are provided, along with an examination of key physical properties derived solely from equilibrium conditions. Interactions contribute to the presence of multiple solutions for the distribution function, as well as an increased particle number, and the presence of plasmons and particles with quantized mass.

This study investigates the application of tensor-train networks in enhancing the performance of analysis-by-synthesis speech recognition. In our model, the analysis transform consists of a convolutional neural network using a sparse transform, while the synthesis transform is a combination of a convolutional neural network and a tensor-train network. The core innovation lies in the integration of a tensor-train network in the synthesis transform of the hybrid model, where its three-dimensional tensors compress the speech feature into a low-rank structure. This approach is further optimized through a two-step training process, where the coefficients of the tensor-train network are fine-tuned using gradient descent and an efficient backpropagation algorithm. In comparison to other hybrid models, our proposed model achieves significant improvements in low-resource settings, especially in terms of fast adaptation and low latency.

We introduce a general approach for deriving quantum-jump evolution equations from three distinct master equation forms in open quantum systems. By leveraging these forms, we derive novel dissipation terms that enable the development of novel and optimized quantum-jump evolution equations. We demonstrate this approach by deriving new jump terms from three established master equation forms. Furthermore, we highlight the utility of this approach in designing optimal quantum-jump based evolution equations and present a protocol for using machine learning to design novel quantum-jump terms, grounded in this approach.

This study explores the influence of plasmonic aluminum nanostructures on silicon solar cell efficiency, examining various structures including spheres, hexagonal prisms, pentagonal prisms, and other prismatic forms. We've investigated how these structures' dimensions, such as particle size and spacing, impact solar cell performance. Our findings reveal that specific geometric shapes like hexagonal prisms and pentagonal prisms lead to better absorption outcomes. Notably, using structures that exhibit quasi-transverse magnetic resonance leads to even better absorption results. We've also identified the optimal size and spacing for these structures to maximize absorption, significantly increasing the phenomenon and potentially doubling the absorption capacity of thin-film solar cells.

The study of evaluating first-order logic with interval and Boolean variable bindings has been carried out, with an emphasis on PTIME logic without counting constructs. This analysis was done by examining how the pullback operation, which is a fundamental algebraic concept, relates to the ability to compute polynomial-time functions in a logic without counting. Specifically, pullbacks were found to be limited in their capacity to capture polynomial-time functions when the input domain consists of integers, with certain implications for the ability to capture polynomial-time functions in a logic without counting in its general form. This led to the classification of logic constructs that can and cannot be used to capture polynomial-time functions in a logic without counting.

Deep learning models, specifically those using LSTMs for video processing, are often too large to fit on a single chip, necessitating distributed processing. Existing distributed LSTM networks, however, are power-hungry due to their redundant computations. To address this, we've developed an algorithm that eliminates unnecessary computations by reusing shared weights across different layers and time steps. We've integrated this algorithm into a hardware accelerator that combines a tensor train decomposition with a distributed architecture, allowing it to be trained in either centralized or distributed settings. Moreover, our hardware can be integrated into deep learning frameworks as a plug-and-play module. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach reduces energy consumption by 3.4 times and data transmission by 1.1 times, all while maintaining performance levels.

The MAVLink protocol, widely used in unmanned aerial systems (UAS) such as the ArduPilot and PX4 projects, enables easy data exchange and communication.  However, its lack of current security measures leaves it vulnerable to attacks.  This research examines MAVLink's security features and proposes a secure framework that can be applied to UAS to prevent potential threats.  Our findings indicate that secure versions of MAVLink can be created by extending existing protocols and suggest several enhancements to mitigate various attack vectors.  Additionally, a proof-of-concept security extension for MAVLink is developed using an ArduPilot-based UAS as an example.

Emulating a network's layout and data flow is essential for developing new network systems, security measures, and research studies.  Kollaps is a decentralized network emulation platform, offering the benefits of central infrastructure, accurate pipeline simulation, and the ability to emulate a wide array of fixed and dynamic network topologies.  This article presents Kollaps' architecture, describes its critical components, and showcases its capabilities with several emulations and relevant research studies that demonstrate its adaptability.  We also discuss the challenges Kollaps faces in achieving precise emulation and the platform's potential limitations.

We previously introduced a unique mapping between specific solutions of Einstein's theory and a particular set of Maxwell's equations in four dimensions. This mapping's properties were explored, particularly in relation to its behavior over time and within asymptotic regions. We now provide an alternative, more intuitive understanding of the mapping and extend it to include solutions that involve multiple light particles propagating at fixed speeds and those with varying speeds.

We've developed a muon detector to map the underground structure of a large, 1.5-kilometer-deep rock cave system using cosmic rays and muons. The muons' high penetration power enables us to create detailed, high-resolution 3D images of the cave system's internal geometry by measuring the angle of arrival of muons created from cosmic rays interacting with air and the surrounding rock. The detector consists of a rotating plastic scintillator with 8 photomultiplier tubes, mounted above the cave system and turned in steps to map the surrounding area. Each step captures the muons' angles of arrival in relation to the observer. The resulting images are created from the combined data collected during the entire scan using a custom-made algorithm. The images provide clear details of the cave system's internal structures, including the outlines and positions of air-filled passages, as well as the shapes and positions of rocks and other obstructions.

This study introduces an updated GLL parsing method capable of parsing not only traditional top-down grammars but also left-most left recursive ones. The new approach maintains the original GLL algorithm's efficiency, avoids over-generated alternates, and allows parsing expressions to generate parsing results directly, eliminating the need to create parser classes. The implementation is available in C# and C++ and can be applied in various settings.

This research investigates the emission of vacuum Cherenkov radiation in the $SU(N_c)$ Yang--Mills theory, considering both temperature-dependent and temperature-independent gauge interactions. Utilizing the Hard Thermal Loop (HTL) approximation, we derive the thermodynamic potential and the effective potential for gluon modes, treating the electromagnetic Cherenkov radiation as a reference. An analytical solution for the critical temperature at which Cherenkov radiation becomes possible is determined, along with the Cherenkov angle for massless gauge fields. The obtained results are then compared with those of temperature-independent gauge interactions.

A key area of investigation in the computational modeling of language is centered on the predictive capabilities of the brain, drawing from Nigro et al.'s (2006) groundbreaking study. Despite the potential of neural networks in addressing this inquiry, their application has been hindered by a limitation: the computational expense associated with testing them on extensive linguistic data. To overcome this obstacle, we developed an efficient deep neural network approach that leverages the strengths of GPU-based processing and the advances in sequence-to-sequence modeling as exemplified by the Transformer model. This approach enables the implementation of a wide range of predictive models on large datasets, thereby facilitating an in-depth examination of the brain's predictive abilities. To validate our method, we employed it to reanalyze the data from Nigro et al.'s study and found that our approach successfully recaptured the critical features of their model. Furthermore, we applied our method to a new, more comprehensive set of data collected from native English speakers as they performed a reading comprehension task. The results of our study underscore the importance of combining large-scale predictive modeling with cutting-edge computational techniques to gain a deeper understanding of the human brain's language processing abilities.

Our research introduces a new method for training pose estimation models that
learns directly from 3D animations without relying on ground truth labels or
synthetic data. We argue that learning from 3D animations should be possible
without the need for corresponding 2D images or ground truth labels. To
demonstrate this, we present a dataset of 3D animations with no paired 2D
information or labels, dubbed "Turntable-300". Our model, designed to predict
3D pose given a single image, utilizes a self-supervised approach that compares
predicted 2D poses to the 3D pose of the object in question. To facilitate
this comparison, we introduce a novel loss function that incorporates the
probability density of 2D poses arising from the object's 3D pose, thereby
enabling learning from 3D to 2D. Our results on the Miniprobe challenge
demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and learning from 2D images of
3D animations proves to be a viable alternative to traditional learning from
2D-3D paired images or ground truth labels.

A novel phenomenon called controlled elastic co-tunneling has been observed in a specially designed semiconductor quantum dot connected by two Andreev bound states through variable superconducting phases. By adjusting the phase differences created by superconducting elements, it is possible to control the flow of electric charge. In addition, the occurrence of a QPC in the quantum dot was found to greatly reduce the effect of elastic co-tunneling. A mathematical model known as the scattering matrix approach was used to explain the behavior of the system.

The transport of energetic particles accelerated by magnetic reconnection is significantly influenced by pitch-angle scattering. We investigate the effect of this scattering on the reconnection rate and the resulting particle distribution, using a mathematical model to represent the scattering process. This model involves the interaction between magnetic fluctuations and energetic particles, leading to an anisotropic scattering effect. We analyze the influence of this scattering effect on both the magnetic field structure and the particle behavior, and provide a mathematical relationship to describe the diffusion coefficient in terms of the particles' energy and pitch-angle. We also derive an equation for the anisotropic scattering rate and apply it to a specific scenario of magnetic reconnection. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our results for the overall understanding of particle acceleration processes.

We investigate the impact of extended scalar sectors on the precision $e^+e^-\to Zh$ and Higgs diphoton rate measurements. In these analyses, a minimal framework is assumed, where the SM higgs field interacts with a set of singlet, doublet, and triplet scalar fields. The unique decay patterns of the SM and additional scalars into $Zh$ and $\gamma\gamma$ are critical to achieving precise cross-section determinations. The results reveal that the extended scalar sectors can be probed with high sensitivity using the precision $e^+e^-\to Zh$ measurement, whereas the Higgs diphoton rate measurement is less effective in this context.
A formula for the subdifferential of the joint numerical radius is developed and utilized to investigate the best approximation problems associated with this quantity.

The growing adoption of the finance sector in Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence has been hindered by a lack of understanding regarding the influence of data protection policies on system performance. We aim to address this issue by exploring the effects of data protection on financial forecasting tasks, leveraging a synthetic dataset to test Differential Privacy algorithms on it and evaluating the trade-off between model accuracy and individual data privacy. Our findings reveal that there is a delicate balance between achieving accurate predictions and preserving the confidentiality of financial data.

This research paper focuses on defining and analyzing stochastic mappings and random distribution fields across filtered probability spaces. A significant aspect of this work explores stochastic mappings between two filtered probability spaces. This concept is further developed by introducing a stochastic operator theory, allowing for an exploration of the inherent properties of random distribution fields. Building on this foundation, the study introduces a novel type of random field, derived from mapping a given field through a stochastic mapping. The investigation culminates in an examination of the statistical characteristics of these newly created random fields.

The existence of ignition in high-pressure hydrogen-helium mixtures under conditions not suitable for focusing a laser beam has been confirmed through experimentation. These experiments utilized a continuous-wave laser and tested mixtures of He, H2, and O2 at pressures ranging from 10 to 50 bar, with a pressure ratio of H2 to O2 of 6. The results show that ignition is possible across a broad range of parameters, with a specific dependence on the input power of the laser and the pressure of the gas mixture. Specifically, this ignition is observed to follow a power law of approximately 3.5 in relation to power and 0.8 in relation to pressure.

Deep learning-based image segmentation has become a prominent technique in various fields. However, traditional models often struggle with capturing the nuances of image boundaries, particularly when dealing with diverse image domains. This paper introduces a boundary-focused image segmentation network, designed to enhance segmentation accuracy and overall image understanding. The proposed framework, consisting of a novel decoder design and a boundary-focused loss function, is adaptable and can be seamlessly integrated into existing image segmentation models. Through comprehensive experiments on multiple standard benchmark datasets, our model exhibits improved boundary detection capabilities and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models in boundary-based evaluations.

This research introduces a driver-messenger system for sharing driving intentions, tested in a simulated lane change context. Our previous work established the importance of such a system, but we now explored implementing it, evaluating its effectiveness with a simulator and gathering real human feedback. We designed a user-friendly interface, integrated it with an automotive-specific input system, and conducted a study with 36 participants, comparing different scenarios. Our results show that communicating driving intentions through the messenger and vehicle systems is perceived as safe, reliable, and beneficial by humans, and preferred over a virtual assistant for information exchange.

This research investigates the impact of boundaries on non-interacting, weakly active particles confined to distinct geometric environments. Our central objective is to determine the equilibrium distribution of these particles within the system. The equilibrium state can be identified by a constant function that remains unchanged over time. For this study, we employ a constant function approach to derive the equilibrium distribution in various container configurations, such as rectangular, curved surface, and semi-circular shapes. The boundary conditions are specified as no active movement at the edges, and the distribution of particles is calculated using the steady-state active diffusion equation.

The extension of the Average Atom Model (AAM) to include Siegert states is explored, which has been crucial in determining the neutron dispersion relations in ultra-dilute gases. The AAM's solution for the Siegret states is obtained by extending the Standard Average Amplitude solution to include states that are inelastic due to a single quantum. The findings reveal that the modified dispersion relations deviate from their elastic counterparts but are nonetheless susceptible to experimental verification. The extension of the AAM to include Siegert states is demonstrated to be a natural progression of the model.

Observations of the Si IV 1398 A doublet in a solar flare were made using the International Space Station-based Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which yielded high-cadence data at 0.18 seconds. Analysis of the data revealed that the line intensity and Doppler shift changed rapidly, within 0.5-1.5 seconds, and were characterized by a series of oscillations lasting around one minute. These oscillations were synchronized with H$\alpha$ flare oscillations and were also observed in other spectral lines. Research on similar flare events suggests that these oscillations are caused by magnetic reconnection in the solar corona. Furthermore, the data showed that the line width increased with plasma temperature, indicating thermal broadening. Calculations using the IRIS spectra and an assumed isothermal plasma revealed a temperature range of 10-100 MK for the observed flare.

A solution to the strong CP problem requires the existence of an global U(1) symmetry, known as Peccei-Quinn symmetry, that is also necessary for inflation. When the symmetry is broken, the axion is a non-perturbative field that is light, with a mass determined by the scale of symmetry breaking. This paper examines the behavior of the axion field near the transition from the inflationary era to the present day, and calculates the density of axion antimatter. It also explores the impact of this density on laboratory experiments and cosmological observations. Notably, the results suggest that a non-minimal axion vacuum could explain the absence of observed dark matter and the observed value of the Hubble constant, and would have a significant effect on the CMB. Furthermore, a future high-precision axion search could provide insight into the early evolution of the universe.

A detailed examination of the angular distribution of sputtered particles emitted from thin films exposed to 30 keV Ar ions reveals specific patterns in which particles are ejected. The distribution appears nearly linear near the angle at which particles seem to flow freely in one direction, however, further investigation via computer simulations suggests this angle is actually dependent on several factors including the film's thickness and the type of atoms making up the film.  The angle at which particles seem to flow freely in one direction is actually a result of the complex interactions of multiple atomic particles and the multiple opportunities for energy transfer that occur as the beam of particles strikes the film.  The detailed interactions of the high-energy particles within the film play a significant role in determining this angle.  The main mechanism for determining this angle is actually the loss of energy by the high-energy particles as they interact with the atoms making up the film.  The detailed interactions of the high-energy particles within the film are found to be crucial in determining the angle.  The detailed interactions of the high-energy particles within the film are found to be crucial in determining the angle at which particles seem to flow freely in one direction.  The detailed interactions of the high-energy particles within the film are examined in more detail.

In our research, we introduce a software tool designed to prevent plagiarism among open-source software developers. The tool analyzes source code by converting program components into vector representations, then generates a query based on these vectors. It ranks relevant code snippets from the query, evaluated against a specified threshold, before storing the top-ranked snippets in a local database. Our approach enables developers to create a plagiarism-detection system utilizing the routing approach without the need for extensive mathematical understanding.

We consider an even integer k, not exceeding 2n-1, and define a series F s, with complex s values, in the following manner: 
F s is equal to the sum over prime number p those of the following expressions: 
$\frac{(-1)^k}{p^{k+1s}}\sum_{\substack{n\in \mathbb{Z},\pm n\leq p}}n^k,
where the summation is restricted to integers n greater than zero, and those equal to minus some positive integer also fall within the range, up to p. 
This work establishes that F s is absolutely convergent for all complex s values with a positive imaginary part, and that F it converges to a Dirichlet L-function, specifically L s over 2, for certain special cases. 
Furthermore, under the assumption that F s is absolutely convergent, we establish that F s is equal to L s over 2, provided that either the imaginary part of s is greater than or equal to one, or s is an even integer with a value less than -1/2. 
Additionally, we establish that F s is equal to L s over 2, for all s values with a positive imaginary part, under the additional condition that the sum over primes of 1/2 valued L functions equals one. 
Finally, we establish that the Dirichlet series F s is uniformly convergent across various rings of

We define the notion of metric approximate subgroups within metric groups.  A metric group along with a real-valued function on the group denoted by $\alpha$ is said to be $\alpha$-stable if any subset $A$ of size $m$ in the group has a subset of size at least $2^Cm$ in $A$ with diameter less than or equal to $\alpha$.  A subset of the group generated by a single element is known as a metric approximate subgroup.  Our main findings are that for any metric approximate subgroup in an ultra-metric group, there exists a bounded function of the subgroup's approximate subgroup generated by $A$ with small $\alpha$ and at most $2^C$ times the cardinality of a subset of the subgroup with bounded Cauchy sequence and diameter less than or equal to $2\alpha$.  This is a higher dimensional version of a result found in ultra-metric approximate groups and a power of a bounded function in groups with bounded generation.  Our proof of this involves the use of a graph argument and a regularized isoperimetric inequality.

In nonparametric statistics, estimating log-concave densities is a significant problem. A widely used approach employs a specific type of discrete distribution derived from the maximum likelihood method applied to a kernel density estimate. However, this method is prone to estimation errors due to its dependence on a small number of observations, leading to inaccurate results. We introduce a new technique that constructs a nonparametric density estimate from a random projective embedding of a point cloud in a high-dimensional space. Unlike existing methods, our approach is capable of accurately estimating log-concave densities even when the data consists of a small number of points. We demonstrate the log-concave property in our method through a geometric proof and show that the estimated density approaches the true density as the dimensionality of the space increases. Furthermore, our approach is computationally efficient and can be implemented using a standard point cloud model. Experimental results also confirm the effectiveness of our method in real-world scenarios.

A novel approach is presented to calculate the entropy of granular systems with irregular shapes by utilizing the Wang-Landau algorithm for sampling static configurations. The method focuses on exploring the space of unique arch structures formed by spheres in granular packing, where each configuration is defined as a minimal set of spheres creating a flat surface. To achieve this, we've developed a customized algorithm that efficiently generates and compares different arch structures based on the initial packing configuration. The proposed method is not only applicable to granular systems, but it's also a starting point for determining the full entropy function for soft-matter systems in a molecular simulation.

The game initiated by Strook involves a director placing tokens on a graph's vertices while an explorer attempts to identify a designated symbol, chosen by the director, by visiting the vertices. This study explores the explorer's best outcome probability and the director's winning strategy, applying the explorer's probability to a series of graphs to find necessary conditions for the director to guarantee victory.

We examine how the correlation between two different frequencies in the time sequence of spectral densities behaves as measurements are taken rapidly, for processes with Gaussian statistics. Distinguishing between cases of strong and weak correlations, we find that a certain type of process can be identified through a power-law relationship in the time sequence of measurements. This analysis also highlights the limitations of a widely used model in accounting for temporal fluctuations in spectral densities.

In this paper, the one-dimensional higher-order Broer-Kaup system is analyzed through a consistent tanh expansion, resulting in the derivation of interaction solutions. Two distinct solutions with varying time parameters are combined to form singular, yet non-symmetric solutions. A distinct characteristic of these solutions is their ability to remain unchanged in certain parameter configurations. Moreover, the solutions exhibit unique properties such as the persistence of their form, the occurrence of singularities at specific parameter values, and the formation of singular profiles with varying parameter values.

This paper establishes energy conservation for a particular class of incompressible Euler equations' weak solutions. These solutions exhibit spatial and temporal boundedness, however do not satisfy certain structural requirements, and their initial velocity possesses low magnitude. Employing the concept of Lagrangian flow and its associated vorticity yields a significant geometric demonstration that contributes significantly to the proof.

VIRUP is an open-source tool for immersive, interactive analysis of astronomical data in 3D visualization. It is based on Unity and easily integrates with C# programming. Users can access and modify all the project's source code, making it ideal for educational purposes. Our project is built upon SLURP, a related platform. VIRUP is suitable for analysis tasks such as tracking the movement of objects, creating 3D objects from 2D images, and conducting object selection and analysis within the Unity environment. Our project enhances the object selection functionality by allowing for the analysis of objects based on additional parameters. To facilitate the analysis, we employ a tree data structure, enabling the handling of objects with complex hierarchical structures. To enhance the efficiency of spatial queries within large datasets, we employ a spatial index, providing a flexible platform for the easy development of new spatial queries. Our project is centered around the analysis of the galaxy distribution in a cosmological context but is versatile enough to be applied to a wide range of astronomical data.

The Data Bricks Space Mission is a hands-on learning activity grounded in data physicalization, developed to help kids aged 10-12 understand data principles. Through this project, middle school students are introduced to basic data visualization concepts and given the opportunity to design and create their own data visualizations, applying what they have learned. Our research employs a qualitative, phenomenological approach, utilizing semi-structured interviews with students involved in the Data Bricks Space Mission to explore their experiences. Our results indicate that this educational task significantly influenced the students' perception of data and visualizations, leading them to consider data in novel ways and with heightened awareness, especially in relation to space. Our study demonstrates the value of data physicalization in inspiring data literacy among young people.

In Software Defined Networking (SDN) with OpenFlow 1.0, the Centralized Controller dictates the path of traffic by sending Forwarding Instructions to individual switches for each packet. Each switch then forwards packets to its intended destination based on the received instructions and its own forwarding table. Despite this, the actual traffic flow is influenced by the combination of the Controller's instructions and the switch's limited capabilities. This study aims to reveal how the actual traffic flow behaves in the system, especially through the switch's internal routing, by identifying the routes taken by each packet. This involves creating a method to extract the routes taken by packets in a given network, based on the information about the packet's origin, the packet it was generated from, and its destination. This method is used to analyze various traffic patterns generated by different SDN data-plane configurations.

Recent advances in disentangled representation learning have been promising but face the challenge of being difficult to adapt in settings where data is organized relationally. To overcome this, we suggest a novel approach that utilizes relational information to promote disentanglement by minimizing the impact of shared relational features across different task variables. Through the application of a variational autoencoder (VAE) and several other baseline models, our research demonstrates the benefits of this approach in various real-world and synthetic data scenarios in terms of improved task-specific understanding and knowledge transfer capabilities.

The concept of oscillating foils is being explored as a potential approach for harnessing energy from ocean currents and tidal movements, and understanding the interplay between foil movement and wake formation is crucial to improving energy harvesting efficiency. This study employs numerical simulations to investigate the effects of adjusting the phase difference between two foils on their combined performance in ocean currents. The analysis considers various scenarios, including identical foil movements and delayed activation, and assesses the relationship between power output and phase difference in the absence of wake interference. It also examines the impact of drag reduction and power gain when multiple foils are used in tandem, and evaluates the validity of these findings by comparing them to theoretical speed reduction predictions.

We've created a cutting-edge, data-driven technique to analyze the real-time evolution of quantum fields during the initial stages of high-energy collisions. By leveraging Bayesian modeling, our approach allows us to accurately predict the state of a system at any point in time, utilizing prior knowledge to minimize uncertainty and ensure physical coherence. Through simulations, we demonstrate the potential of this method in determining the non-equilibrium behavior of quark gluon plasma, and its insights regarding the early stages of thermalization.

We have developed a method to observe the interaction between a quantum dot and a superconducting island through voltage sensing. By applying this technique, we were able to detect both coherent tunneling and incoherent tunneling processes. Our findings, specifically regarding the coherence between incoherent tunneling rates, suggest that our technique is capable of providing insight into charge tunneling mechanisms and may even detect the presence of coherent processes that would otherwise be missed.

The development of new drugs is a time-consuming process that requires extensive research. To expedite the process, computational methods based on generative models can be utilized to predict new drug candidates. Our research focuses on a dataset comprising 1022 approved drugs. We examine the effectiveness of three distinct energy-based models: Energy-based Generative Model, Jensen-Shannon-based Generative Model, and Weighted Jensen-Shannon-based Generative Model, in generating drugs with specific therapeutic indications. The results reveal that the Weighted Jensen-Shannon-based Generative Model yields the highest success rate of 34.81%, indicating that it can successfully produce target-specific drugs. A comprehensive analysis is provided for both the model and the dataset.

The Graph Graph Rewriting (GGR) approach, a dynamic geometry of interaction machine, employs graph rewriting as a means of evaluating terms. This is achieved through the use of a variable collection, a term graph, and a set of reduction rules that determine the rewriting graph's topological structure. In contrast to static geometry of interaction machines, GGR introduces a dynamic approach by only allowing reduction at variable bindings. Terms are represented as token graphs, and variable bindings are defined by edges between these tokens. This results in a natural, context-dependent substitution mechanism, where each substitution graph is generated within the term graph via a reduction rule. This graph rewriting graph (GGR) serves as the foundation for GGR, allowing for an interactive and dynamic rewriting process. This paper introduces the GGR machine, demonstrating its ability to execute reduction rules with explicit substitution, and discussing its relationship to both traditional substitution models and the dynamic geometry of interaction machine.

We've analyzed the motion of stars in the outer LMC region, using precise proper motion data from the VMC survey, and identified distinct populations based on their chemical composition. Our research confirms the existence of an LMC disk and an X-shaped structure, and reveals a significant star cluster at the LMC center. Additionally, we've found evidence of tidal streams within the SMC and their impact on the LMC's evolution. Our study's key discoveries are as follows: 
1. The LMC's disk exhibits a blue, red-blue, and red color-magnitude diagram, and its X-shaped structure shows blue, red-blue, and red stars. 
2. The stars within the LMC's disk and X-shaped structure show different proper motion patterns, which are similar to those of the SMC's anti-center region. 
3. The stars within the SMC region show a distinct proper motion pattern, which is separate from the LMC's populations, and their motion can be explained by the LMC's motion towards the SMC. 
4. The SMC's tidal structure is primarily influenced by the SMC's own tidal radius, and its star populations within the LMC region show a significant overlap with the LMC's populations, which are predominantly influenced by the LMC's disk.

Advanced smart grid systems known as Advanced Metering Infrastructure are being used to boost their efficiency. Yet, their security is at risk due to the capability of hackers to breach them. This vulnerability is exploited by hackers to steal electricity, causing significant financial losses for both households and power companies. Traditional methods for detecting and preventing electricity theft are often based on outdated information and don't account for the complex relationships in the smart grid. A new approach is proposed in this paper to detect electricity theft using deep learning techniques. A deep neural network is used to create a model that can identify patterns in electricity usage before and after theft, and classify them as either genuine or fake theft. This classification is based on the assumption that genuine theft will have different patterns in electricity usage than fake theft. To improve the accuracy of this model, the number of hidden layers and neurons in each layer are adjusted through a process called random hyperparameter tuning. A large dataset of 120,000 smart grid records was used to train and test this model. The results show that this model achieves 99.2% accuracy in detecting electricity theft, with a recall of 99.7% and an F1 score of 99.5%.

We define the concept of the Menger number for compact metric spaces and show that compact subsets of the 2-dimensional sphere with finite Menger number yield tight surface graphs. Additionally, for any integer greater than or equal to 4, we construct an infinite set of tight surface graphs each having a Menger number of that specific integer.

Measurements of hadron production in high-energy collisions are crucial for understanding the strong interaction between quarks.  A new study presents the first measurements of the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons' lifetimes, obtained from data collected at the LHCb experiment in 2016.  A unique method was employed to isolate the background from non-corrected data, and the results show that these two baryons have significantly longer lifetimes than previously suggested by the Particle Data Group, with values of $1.33\pm 0.20\pm 0.08$ ps and $1.600\pm 0.040\pm 0.048$ ps respectively, at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV.

This paper introduces an innovative, fast, and accurate framework for unsupervised hyperspectral image classification, integrating the principles of spatial aggregation, similarity-based subspace clustering, and label prediction. Initially, a spatial aggregation network is employed to leverage local contextual information within hyperspectral images, producing spatially enhanced features. These enhanced features are then fed into a similarity-based subspace clustering network, utilizing a novel distance metric and cluster assignment strategy to group samples of the same class together. Finally, a label prediction network is utilized to assign labels to each pixel of the hyperspectral image, and the results are evaluated on four benchmark hyperspectral images, yielding superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Arctic sea ice features undulations with a significant impact on its properties, 
specifically melting and snow accumulation, which are influenced by these 
undulations. An idealized model, the snow dune model, is capable of predicting 
the complex interactions between heat transfer and snow accumulation without 
relying on intricate interplay between thermal and hydraulic processes. 
Research demonstrates that this model accurately forecasts the prevalence, 
height, and spacing of snow-covered undulations observed on flat, unaltered Arctic 
sea ice and shows that these features are primarily driven by the combined 
effects of heat loss due to long-wave radiation and wind-induced snow accumulation 
as opposed to thermal convection.

We investigate the quantum Zeno effect in ultracold atom-molecule collisions within a static and time-varying magnetic field. Our results show that a high-frequency probing field can significantly reduce or halt the process of quantum tunneling by continuously measuring the spin of the molecules using laser pulses. This effect is highly dependent on the probe field's frequency and amplitude, as well as the strength of the intermolecular interaction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the quantum Zeno effect can be controlled by adjusting the probe field's characteristics and the magnetic field's orientation.

We establish that the nonextensive It\^o-Langevin dynamics, a generalization of It\^o-Langevin dynamics where particle velocities follow a q-exponential distribution, can be derived from a broader statistical mechanics framework based on the q-deformed central limit theorem, a more general statistical hypothesis. This approach encompasses the conventional statistical mechanics and fluctuation statistics, and we examine its underlying principles and results in depth. Specifically, we show that the stationary state of this dynamics, a Gibbs-like distribution, is a natural outcome when minimizing the equilibrium free energy under the constraints of a fixed total energy and momentum. Moreover, we find that the time evolution of this Gibbs-like distribution aligns with the q-deformed central limit theorem.

The emergence of non-Abelian Weyl nodes, which have a topological origin, is significant in condensed matter physics research. Our study reveals that a higher-order topological Weyl node can form under basic light exposure in a classically understood semimetal called $\mathcal{C}_3$. This semimetal's response to the optical drive leads to the formation of a closed nodal line where energy levels touch, causing a gapless band structure. Applying a weak optical field then breaks time-reversal and inversion symmetries, causing the initial gapless band to split into distinct bands with non-zero Chern numbers. This results in the formation of two separate Weyl nodes, each featuring a different order of topology, with the first featuring a single Weyl point and the second featuring a four-fold Weyl point. This research demonstrates that a non-Abelian Weyl node can be created under basic optical stimulation in a semimetal, with the possibility of experimental realization using a diamond material.

This paper presents a decentralized computing protocol on a blockchain, called Marvel DC, that empowers users to selectively share their computing resources with others. Our analysis indicates that this protocol fulfills requirements for decentralized and incentive-compatible computation sharing, and its security is safeguarded against cheating and unauthorized access.

A new, reduced-reference perceptual rate-distortion model has been developed for 3D point cloud compression, specifically designed for interactive applications. This model uses features extracted from sparse, compressed data and a deep learning-based regression network to predict the structural loss and distortion error without accessing original images. Experimental results show that the model's performance is close to that of a full-reference perceptual metric. Moreover, when incorporated into a rate-distortion-contrastive framework, this model enables the creation of compressed 3D point clouds that are semantically similar to their original counterparts.

Research on holography and its application to complex matter states has shown significant progress. This contribution examines a holographic approach to understanding the QCD phase diagram, focusing on the phase transitions that occur between a confined hadronic phase and a deconfined phase of quarks and gluons. Key aspects include the temperature-dependent crossover between these phases, the first-order phase transition that occurs at a critical chemical potential, and the resulting critical behavior. Additionally, the holographic investigation explores the baryon-mass dependence of the phase transition and the behavior of compact baryons across different temperature ranges. It also examines the phase transitions in rotating baryonic matter. Furthermore, the holographic approach is used to model the hadronic phase, employing a vector meson potential. Lastly, the contribution discusses the limitations and unresolved issues of the holographic approach and proposes potential directions for future research.

The use of MRI for diagnosing knee abnormalities, including injuries and osteoarthritis, has gained attention in recent years. However, MRI assessments remain largely subjective and time-consuming, necessitating innovative solutions. Our research presents a novel, self-supervised transformer network that can automatically identify knee abnormalities from MRI scans, without requiring any subject-specific training. Our model leverages a 3D slice-based approach, incorporating global and local context information through hierarchical attention and a patch mixture strategy. Our method achieves a high diagnostic accuracy, matching that of the best supervised methods, even when trained on a limited dataset.

This research focuses on few-shot font generation, aiming to produce new fonts given just a small sample of three fonts. The key challenge lies in capturing and representing the intricate styles of different fonts, even when their classification under the same font family is identical. We address this problem by introducing a novel approach that extracts and learns the distinct styles of individual glyphs, which can be combined to generate new fonts. The proposed method involves three primary components: 1) a glyph-style representation model, 2) a style integration module, and 3) a novel loss function. Through extensive testing on various font classification systems, the results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, especially in generating new fonts with unique styles. The code for our research will be made publicly available.

We've discovered that in a fluid in equilibrium with its surroundings, certain geometrical anomalies can induce unique effects. These effects arise from a specific type of symmetry known as in-out-translational symmetry, which causes the material's properties to vary depending on the chosen frame of reference. This particular anomaly leads to an observable phenomenon when it is broken spontaneously, resulting in the development of a torsional anomaly. This torsional anomaly produces an anomalous contribution to the fluid's stress-energy tensor, which depends on the chosen frame and a torsional order parameter. It also gives rise to a torsional version of the Wess-Zumino term, appearing at the two-loop order in the effective action. Furthermore, we've found that the torsional anomaly allows for the definition of a geometric charge, analogous to the 't Hooft anomaly, which can be measured by introducing a boundary and evaluating the stress-energy tensor on that boundary.

This paper presents a novel approach to personalized video streaming, tailored to balance the individual QoE of each user in a multi-user environment. By employing a digital twin-based adaptive video framework, it enables real-time performance analysis and optimized content adaptation for each user. A dynamic model-driven method is used to forecast and mitigate potential adverse effects on QoE, particularly buffer underruns and long start times, while a content-based model is utilized to enhance the visual quality of each user by selecting the most suitable video format. Furthermore, the framework utilizes an online learning mechanism, leveraging the least squares support vector machine regression, to continuously refine the prediction accuracy of the digital twin-based adaptive video model throughout the streaming process. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed approach's ability to significantly boost the visual quality of the video and the individual QoE of the users without compromising buffer performance.

The verification of astrophysical $\gamma$-ray emission theories necessitates the detection of ultra-high energy neutrinos and cosmic rays. The future km-scale underwater Cherenkov telescopes, KM3NeT/Straw and KM3NeT/Arca, aim to achieve the required energy and angular resolution to identify neutrino-induced cascades originating from tau-leptons in the presence of a substantial background from bioluminescent organisms. To achieve this goal, a double cascade reconstruction method has been developed that enhances the success rate of tau-induced cascade identification by a significant margin, as demonstrated in simulations of neutrino interactions with sea ice and ice in the DeepCore scenario.

The study focuses on a nonlinear periodic Schrödinger equation with nonlocal exponent 2, which incorporates a white noise term representing dispersion. To address this complex problem, a novel approach called the 'parabolic approximation method' is developed, which yields a positive Prokhorov dimension bound. Furthermore, by leveraging this bound, the study demonstrates the well-definedness of a nonlinear stochastic wave equation solutions in higher-dimensional scenarios.

Ensuring the reliability of wireless communication in complex systems, especially those with latency constraints, is crucial. This paper addresses the joint scheduling and coding problem for real-time data transfer over multiple parallel wireless channels. The main focus is on developing a reliable scheduling scheme that leverages channel diversity to achieve minimum required data transfer rates while limiting delays. The problem is formulated under different assumptions regarding channel state information, link quality, and data requirements. The paper derives fundamental bounds on achievable delays and develops efficient algorithms that approximate scheduling solutions for various channel models. The proposed algorithms are validated through simulation results and demonstrated on a wireless sensor node.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant is situated near the center of the Milky Way galaxy, particularly close to the supermassive black hole located at the galaxy's core. A detailed X-ray and infrared image analysis led to the identification of a previously unseen compact source within the remnant's eastern edge. This newly discovered source shares the same radio shape as Sgr A East, suggesting it may be responsible for the observed asymmetry in the region. A possible scenario to account for the source's characteristics involves a nearby supernova explosion that occurred within a nearby molecular cloud, situated approximately 0.1-0.3 parsecs away from the center of the galaxy. This event would have the dual effect of positioning the remnant's newly discovered source in the correct location, while also explaining the observed radio asymmetry. A more recent, approximately 10,000 year old supernova would have allowed sufficient time for the shock wave to travel across the cloud, resulting in the observed radio shape.
